quote: <div className="timeline" dir="ltr" ref={scroller} onWheel={onWheel} style={{ overflowX: "auto" }}>
title: Playback timeline pinned LTR — does not mirror in RTL, violates STYLING.md
problem: The timeline root hard-codes dir="ltr", so in an RTL locale (Arabic, Hebrew) the whole strip keeps its left-to-right scroll origin, tick order and progress growth while every other surface on the page mirrors. STYLING.md states the project rule: "Layout is direction-agnostic: use logical properties ... Never hard-code a writing direction." This line is a direct, unambiguous breach of that rule, and the same component is the only one in src/player that forces a direction on a scrolling surface the user interacts with. RTL users get a page whose primary control sits on the wrong side of the visual flow and whose progress moves against the reading direction of everything around it.
impact: Trigger: a user whose locale is ar or he opens the player. Outcome: the timeline renders and scrolls left-to-right inside a mirrored page; it looks broken and inconsistent, and the project's own styling rule is violated in shipped code. Accessibility reviewers will flag the same thing.
suggested_fix: Remove dir="ltr" from the timeline root and compute scroll offsets with logical properties (scrollInlineStart / writing-mode aware offsets). Delete the lint exemption for src/player/PlaybackTimeline.tsx in eslint.config.js so the logical-properties rule applies here like everywhere else.
evidence: STYLING.md line 3; eslint.config.js has to carry a special exemption to keep this line, which shows the rule is being worked around rather than followed.

title: Wheel seek ignores the scroller's scroll offset
problem: onWheel converts the pointer position to media time with e.clientX - rect.left only. The strip is a horizontally scrolling element (overflowX: auto) whose content is wider than its box, so the pixel under the pointer is rect-relative position PLUS scroller.scrollLeft. Without scrollLeft the computed time is always inside the first viewport-width of the media.
impact: Trigger: the user scrolls the timeline past the first screen and wheels over it. Outcome: onSeek jumps back to a time in the first few seconds instead of the time under the pointer.
suggested_fix: Use const x = e.clientX - rect.left + e.currentTarget.scrollLeft.
evidence: The effect on line 18-21 maps positionMs to scrollLeft with the same PX_PER_SECOND, so the two directions are inconsistent.

title: Resize listener is never removed
problem: The effect registers a window resize listener and returns no cleanup. It re-registers every time positionMs changes (several times a second during playback) and is never removed on unmount, so listeners accumulate and each keeps a stale closure and the unmounted element alive.
impact: Trigger: playback for a few minutes, or mounting and unmounting the timeline. Outcome: hundreds of resize handlers run on every resize, and the detached scroller is retained (leak).
suggested_fix: Return () => window.removeEventListener("resize", onResize) from the effect.
evidence: No removeEventListener anywhere in the file.

title: Icon-only mute button has no accessible name
problem: The button's only content is an emoji glyph. Screen readers announce it as a speaker-with-cancellation-stroke emoji or nothing at all, and there is no aria-label, title or visually hidden text. The sibling controls in MediaPlaybackControls.tsx all carry aria-label.
impact: Trigger: a screen-reader user tabs to the volume control. Outcome: they cannot tell what the button does (WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value).
